Figure 1:A bimanual robot is two arms, not one arm with
twice the joints.Left: existing tokenizers treat the two arms as a single arm and mix theleftandrightarm in every token; BiCAT gives
each arm its own token stream, aware of its partner.
Right: BiCAT rollouts on three embodiments with each arm’s motion over
time, and success rates in simulation and on real robots; white numbers
give the gain over the best baseline.

Figure 2:Overview of BiCAT. Top: mirror canonicalization𝒞\mathcal{C}flips the signed joints of the right arm (q1,…,q7q_{1},\ldots,q_{7}, withq7q_{7}the
gripper) and applies shared normalization; the shared encoderEϕE_{\phi}and causal cross-attention give each arm its partner’s context before FSQ;
and the joint decoderDθD_{\theta}reconstructs the canonical chunk underℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}, which𝒞−1\mathcal{C}^{-1}maps back to𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}}. Bottom: a VLM predicts𝐲L\mathbf{y}^{L}, then𝐲R\mathbf{y}^{R}; the frozen decoder returns actions, executed on
Bimanual SO-101, Unitree G1, and Bimanual YAM. Teal: left arm; orange:
right arm.
Figure 4:BiCAT rollouts on three real bimanual embodiments.Each row shows four keyframes of one task with a short task description.

Figure 5:Overview of the ten RoboTwin evaluation tasks.

Figure 6:t-SNE of pre-quantization arm latents on the ten RoboTwin 2.0
tasks. Each point is one arm of one action chunk, averaged over its eight
latent positions; each panel contains the same 10,000 chunks. Red and
blue shades denote the left and right arms. Each panel is fitted
separately, so coordinates and distances are not comparable across
panels; the left–right MMD reported in the text is computed in the
original latent space.
